problem_shape: These papers share a marketplace problem: a platform must decide what product, ad, price, coupon, page layout, campaign, or answer to put in front of a person while money, attention, trust, and inventory are all limited. A shopping site does not merely retrieve matching items. It has to guess whether a person will click, buy, return, abandon, compare across shops, accept a delivery promise, or be harmed by unsafe advertising. An advertising system has the same pressure with a different surface: it must spend a budget over channels and moments before the final value is fully known. The input evidence shows this pressure across 152 papers, with many examples in WWW and SIGIR and smaller groups in WSDM and KDD. The family belongs together because each paper treats commerce as a repeated allocation problem under partial evidence. The system sees queries, images, catalog fields, prices, bids, clicks, conversions, refunds, seller behavior, ad content, and experiment results, then must turn those fragments into a choice that affects buyers, sellers, advertisers, and the platform.
naive_failure: A smart beginner would rank by the most obvious signal: show visually similar products for an image query, favor items with many clicks, spend more where recent sales were high, suppress risky results when a model score is low, or trust an A/B test when one version wins. Those rules fail because commerce feedback is delayed, mixed, and shaped by the platform itself. A click can happen long before a purchase, and a purchase can later be refunded. An item-level score can miss the fact that the same product at a different price behaves differently. Popular products and strong sellers get more exposure because they were already exposed. Ads compete for attention beside other ads. A layout change can alter where people look, not just what they prefer. Scam campaigns rotate content and hide behind harmless-looking material. In this family, the simple score is usually too flat for the decision it controls.
mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is controlled decision-making from incomplete feedback. In plain terms, the system builds a score for each possible action, but it also asks what that score is allowed to mean. Conversion papers estimate chances: given this user, item, price, and time, how likely is a click, purchase, refund, delivery delay, or booking? Ranking papers sort candidates, but the order must balance relevance, variety, page position, visual evidence, long-term satisfaction, and business value. Bidding and budget papers choose settings by defining what counts as wrong, such as spending too fast, underspending, violating a coupon constraint, or missing conversions, then adjusting decisions to reduce that wrongness. Causal papers compare like with like so the platform does not confuse a decision that caused a sale with a decision merely shown near a likely sale. Testing papers use repeated experiments to estimate whether a change is real or noise. Safety and anomaly papers compare current content or prediction patterns with expected patterns, then flag sharp departures. The tradeoff is accuracy versus cost, revenue versus user welfare, fast action versus delayed truth, and personalization versus unfair or unsafe exposure.
why_math_matters: The math matters because online commerce has structure that ordinary rules leave unused. A booking path has stages: a person may search, click, consider substitutes, book, or leave. A campaign has language that may point only indirectly to product types. A product has text, image, brand, price, stock status, seller offers, and sometimes many near-duplicate variants. A budget has time: money spent early cannot be spent later, but waiting too long may miss valuable moments. These structures make the data less like a pile of independent facts and more like a set of connected clocks, funnels, and scarce slots. Probability is useful because final outcomes arrive late and unevenly. Ranking is useful because the platform can show only a few things. Control and planning are useful because bids and budgets must be adjusted while feedback is still arriving. Careful testing is useful because many users and sellers behave differently, and parallel experiments can interfere with each other. The papers need these tools to separate signal from exposure, timing, layout, price, and strategic behavior.
paper_family: The representative papers are different branches of the same deeper move: make the marketplace choice more faithful before acting on it. CASCADE separates conversion and refund timing instead of pretending net conversion is immediately visible. Price SKU modeling says a product cannot be scored only at item level when price variants change behavior. ARCHER, MMRM, MCRec, catalog-quality work, and campaign-to-product attribution all repair the meaning match between queries, images, brand knowledge, campaigns, covers, and products. STCRank, whole-page search, demand-calibrated facet diversification, and CoCo focus on the order or suppression decision: what should be shown, where, and with how much confidence? DARA, GAM, AHBid, TAR, ZIPBid, and small-budget feedback control treat advertising as a paced sequence of spending choices under constraints. Prediction Guardian, scam-campaign anatomy, unsafe YouTube advertising detection, brand-safety detection, EVADE-Bench, and the hidden energy-cost study add the trust branch: commercial systems must notice corruption, evasion, inappropriate ads, and costs pushed onto users. AgenticShop, ACES, WebMall, Click-to-Ask, and live-shopping assistants show a newer interface where agents and language systems help shop, compare, ask, choose, and sell across marketplaces with live context.
what_changed: The 2026 version of this family is less about a single click predictor and more about commerce systems that must reason across richer surfaces. The evidence shows price-level conversion, refund delay, whole-page layout, spatial ad interactions, multimodal product ranking, live-stream question answering, catalog repair, multi-shop agent evaluation, and agentic buying behavior. Large language models appear often, but mostly as interpreters, planners, assistants, or label builders rather than magic replacements for marketplace measurement. Another shift is operational pressure: budget pacing, real-time anomaly response, parallel experimentation, sparse feedback, thousands of repeated items, and evasive content all force methods to work under deployment constraints. The common change is broader responsibility for the decision loop, from matching and ranking through spending, safety, measurement, and governance.
limits: The family depends on logged marketplace data being a useful guide to future marketplace behavior. That assumption can fail when past rankings created the evidence, when sellers strategically adapt, when scams change templates, or when an AI shopping agent has different biases from human buyers. Conversion and bidding models can be numerically precise while still optimizing the wrong business or user outcome. A/B tests can reduce false positives, but they do not settle long-term welfare, seller fairness, or effects that spill across experiments. Multimodal and language systems rely on catalog text, images, brand knowledge, and generated labels being accurate enough to trust. The input evidence reports problems, approaches, and contributions, not full deployment proof across all product categories, countries, advertisers, page designs, or adversarial settings.
